bib.title: SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings

question: Can a simple contrastive objective on pre-trained language models produce much better sentence embeddings, with or without labeled data?
hypothesis: Dropout noise alone can serve as minimal data augmentation for a self-prediction contrastive objective; NLI entailment pairs plus contradiction hard negatives further improve alignment; the contrastive objective flattens the anisotropic embedding spectrum.
contributions: Unsupervised SimCSE: predict the sentence itself with two dropout masks as positive pair
Supervised SimCSE: NLI entailment as positives, contradiction as hard negatives
Alignment/uniformity and singular-spectrum analysis linking contrastive learning to anisotropy
Consolidated STS evaluation settings (regressor, Spearman vs Pearson, aggregation)

method.summary: Fine-tune all parameters of pre-trained BERT/RoBERTa with an in-batch-negative cross-entropy contrastive loss on cosine similarity with temperature. Unsupervised: same sentence encoded twice with different dropout masks. Supervised: NLI entailment pairs as positives, contradiction hypotheses as hard negatives.
method.task: sentence embedding learning, evaluated on semantic textual similarity (STS) and transfer tasks

metrics.name: Spearman correlation on STS
metrics.definition: rank correlation between cosine similarity of embeddings and human scores, 'all' aggregation (concatenate subsets)

metrics.name: alignment
metrics.definition: E||f(x)-f(x+)|| squared over positive pairs (STS-B score>4), normalised embeddings

metrics.name: uniformity
metrics.definition: log E exp(-2||f(x)-f(y)||^2) over all STS-B sentences

eval.protocol: STS-B dev used for ablations and checkpoint choice; no STS training data; baselines re-evaluated in same setting where possible; no seeds or significance tests stated

results.claim: Supervised SBERTbase averages 74.89 STS, below supervised SimCSE-BERTbase.
results.setup: SBERTbase, results from Reimers and Gurevych 2019

results.claim: Removing dropout (identical positives) cuts STS-B dev from 82.5 to 71.1; using the same dropout mask on both gives 43.6.
Unsup SimCSE beats next-sentence objectives (82.5 vs 67.4 on STS-B dev) and discrete augmentations such as deleting one word (75.9).
Dropout 0.1 is best for unsup SimCSE; 0.5 gives 71.0.
NLI entailment pairs are the best positives (84.9 full) versus QQP 81.8, Flickr30k 81.4, ParaNMT 78.7.
results.setup: BERTbase STS-B dev, same hyperparameters as final model
results.table: Table 4, row SNLI+MNLI entailment (314k), column full

results.claim: NLI entailment pairs have 39% lexical overlap (F1 of bags of words), versus 60% for QQP and 55% for ParaNMT.
Adding contradiction hypotheses as hard negatives lifts STS-B dev from 84.9 to 86.2.
Neutral hypotheses as extra hard negatives give no gain (85.3 vs 86.2).
A dual-encoder variant of supervised SimCSE hurts (86.2 to 84.2).
Temperature matters: tau=0.05 gives 86.2, tau=1 gives 64.0; dot product gives 85.9.
Post-processing (flow, whitening) improves uniformity but degrades alignment; SimCSE improves uniformity while keeping alignment, and supervised data further improves alignment.
results.setup: alignment/uniformity plot of BERTbase-based models, STS-B pairs; no numeric values printed in text

results.claim: Pre-trained embeddings have good alignment but poor uniformity, i.e. they are highly anisotropic.
SimCSE gives more spread cosine similarities across human-rated STS-B similarity groups than BERT/SBERT, with lower variance on similar pairs than whitening.
results.setup: STS-B pairs grouped by rating, density plots, Fig G.1

results.claim: SimCSE is not sensitive to batch size when learning rate is tuned, contradicting the claim that contrastive learning needs large batches.
results.setup: grid over batch 64-512, lr 1e-5 to 5e-5, STS-B dev; pre-trained init suggested as cause

results.claim: BERT-flow/whitening post-processing hurt SentEval transfer performance relative to base models; STS results alone do not predict transfer.
results.setup: Appendix E, no numbers printed in text

results.claim: Published STS papers use incoherent protocols (regressor, Pearson/Spearman, all/mean/wmean aggregation); e.g. SBERT average is 74.85 under all and 73.55 under wmean.
results.table: Table B.2, row SBERT (wmean), column Avg.

limits: Evaluation is mainly STS (symmetric sentence similarity) and SentEval; no retrieval benchmark such as BEIR or passage retrieval; only a qualitative 150k-caption Flickr30k retrieval example.
Authors concede STS gains need not transfer: flow/whitening hurt transfer tasks, MLM helps transfer but hurts STS.
Ablations use STS-B dev, which is also used for checkpoint selection and hyperparameter grid search.
Single runs; no seeds or significance tests stated.
English only; sentences, not documents or queries vs passages.
Hardware, compute, optimizer, warmup and schedule, max sequence length not stated.
Anisotropy argument (Jensen bound) is asymptotic in number of negatives and assumes positive similarities.
